title: Molecular mechanisms and clinical insights in transformed small cell lung cancer: a narrative review
author: Xianzi Dai; Yue Hao; Jiaojiao Hong; Jiangxia Yuan; Chengyu Chen; Zhengxing Huo; Jia Zhu; Qian Wang
text:
Abstract
Background and Objective
In recent years, the application of targeted therapies has significantly improved survival rates in patients with driver gene-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, one mechanism underlying acquired resistance is the histological transformation from NSCLC to small cell lung cancer (SCLC). NSCLC-to-SCLC transformation is thought to occur due to selective pressure from targeted therapies, yet this shift has also been observed in patients receiving non-targeted treatments, raising questions about its underlying mechanisms. This review aims to identify key molecular biomarkers predictive of this transformation to optimize clinical management strategies for transformed SCLC (T-SCLC).
Methods
We systematically searched PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and major international conference proceedings for all English-language articles published up to December 31, 2024. This review synthesizes current evidence on the mechanisms of T-SCLC transformation, its genomic and transcriptomic alterations, and related therapeutic approaches.
Key Content and Findings
T-SCLC is hypothesized to involve tumor heterogeneity and lineage plasticity. Key molecular players include dysregulation of the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT)/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, NOTCH-ASCL1 signaling, mothers against decapentaplegic homolog 4 (SMAD4), SRY-related HMG-box 2 (SOX2), and epigenetic abnormalities such as histone modifications (methylation, acetylation, ubiquitination). Tumor protein p53 (TP53) and retinoblastoma 1 (RB1) inactivation may serve as predictive biomarkers, though causal relationships require validation. Post-transformation, chemotherapy remains the first-line treatment, while combining chemotherapy with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) improves progression-free survival.
Conclusions
Current T-SCLC research is limited by retrospective designs and small sample sizes, leaving transformation mechanisms incompletely understood. This phenotypic shift highlights lung cancer plasticity as a novel resistance mechanism rooted in lineage plasticity and tumor heterogeneity. Personalized therapies guided by molecular profiling may represent a future direction for improving outcomes.
Keywords: Transformed small cell lung cancer (T-SCLC), acquired drug resistance profile, plasticity
Introduction
Lung cancer is one of the most prevalent and deadly malignant tumors worldwide, with the highest rates of morbidity and mortality (1). Histologically, lung cancer is classified into two subtypes: non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC), which account for approximately 85% and 15% of lung cancer patients, respectively. Molecular targeted therapies have significantly improved the survival and prognosis of advanced NSCLC patients with positive driver gene mutations. Meanwhile, immunotherapy, particularly programmed death protein 1 (PD-1)/programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitors, has revolutionized the treatment of advanced, driver gene-negative NSCLC. However, the inevitable development of acquired drug resistance in both targeted therapy and immunotherapy remains a major clinical challenge in advanced NSCLC (2).
When NSCLC progresses, some cases undergo histological transformation to SCLC, referred to as transformed SCLC (T-SCLC). T-SCLC is one of the mechanisms of acquired resistance to targeted therapies, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy, such as epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) inhibitors, and ROS1 inhibitors (3,4). Several case studies have documented the clinical characteristics of patients with transformed tumors, including their treatment regimens, smoking history, transformation frequency, average time to transformation, and post-transformation survival (Table 1) (5-11). Statistical analyses show that EGFR-mutated lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) patients treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) experience a higher rate of transformation, and a higher proportion of female patients is significantly associated with T-SCLC. Smoking history does not show a significant correlation with transformation, though it is linked to a poorer prognosis. Post-transformation overall survival (OS) is influenced by cancer stage, with patients in the limited stage exhibiting a relatively better prognosis (12,13). Despite these advances, the availability of tumor tissues for analysis before and after SCLC transformation remains limited, and the molecular mechanisms driving this histological transformation are still largely unknown.

The genetic alterations and molecular features between T-SCLC and neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) suggest that insights from one cancer type may offer valuable information for the other. Prostate adenocarcinoma is initially highly responsive to antiandrogen therapy, much like how EGFR-mutant LUAD responds to EGFR inhibitors. However, these therapies only temporarily slow tumor progression, and almost all patients eventually develop acquired resistance (14). In addition, deletion of retinoblastoma 1 (RB1)/tumor protein p53 (TP53) and the overexpression of MYC proto-oncogene (MYC) family genes are commonly observed in most cases of NEPCs, playing a crucial role in lineage plasticity. This molecular signature is also present in T-SCLC, and previous clinical studies in NEPC could offer insights for understanding T-SCLC (15).
Although T-SCLC shares similarity with primary SCLC in terms of pathological features, molecular features, clinical manifestations, and drug sensitivity, its pathogenesis and tumor microenvironment differ significantly from primary SCLC, necessitating distinct treatment approaches. Furthermore, effective treatments for T-SCLC remain limited, further contributing to the poor prognosis of affected patients. This review aims to provide an overview of the latest research on the mechanisms, early detection strategies, and potential treatment options for T-SCLC. We present this article in accordance with the Narrative Review reporting checklist (available at https://tlcr.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tlcr-2025-165/rc).
Methods
We systematically searched PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and major international conference proceedings for all English-language articles published up to December 31, 2024.

Mechanism of formation
Current hypotheses
The first hypothesis is lineage plasticity, commonly referred to as neuroendocrine transdifferentiation (NEtD), which is increasingly recognized as a mechanism of resistance to therapies, particularly molecularly targeted therapies (16). Evidence indicates that SCLCs that arise following targeted therapy often retain the molecular features of the original adenocarcinoma, including EGFR mutations, ALK, and ROS1 fusions. This supports the hypothesis that T-SCLC evolves directly from the original tumor, rather than from de novo tumors (17-19). T-SCLC shares many characteristics with high-grade neuroendocrine tumors, including a high frequency of RB1/TP53 mutations, the presence of neuroendocrine tumor markers, and a transient response to platinum-based chemotherapy regimens (20,21). A study by Sutherland et al. (22) assessed the effects of TP53 and RB1 inactivation in different cell types in the adult lung using adenoviral vectors targeting Cre recombinase. The results showed that alveolar type II cells may also undergo SCLC transformation, albeit at a much lower frequency than neuroendocrine cells. The lineage plasticity hypothesis theory has gained widespread acceptance to date.
The second hypothesis centers on tumor heterogeneity, which includes clonal selection and tumor stem cell theory (23). One view is that several subpopulations of SCLC existed within the tumor prior to anticancer therapy, with specific SCLC subtypes better suited for survival under the selective pressures of treatment. Another view suggests that T-SCLCs arise from NSCLC through stress-induced mutations following treatment. Tumor heterogeneous allow subsets of cell to form drug-resistant clones under the environmental pressure exerted by drugs, facilitating tumor, and the formation of drug-resistant dominant clones. The mechanisms underlying drug resistance, apart from mutations in drug-resistant genes, are often explained by three models: the Darwinian selection model, the Lamarckian induction model, and the coexistence of the two models (24). Xie et al.’s study (25) demonstrated that SCLC differentiation occurs early from the founding clone, with distinct histopathological and tissue-type differentiation observed even at the initial diagnostic stage, showing inactivation of both TP53 and RB1 genes in NSCLC. Most studies agree that the transformation of EGFR-mutated NSCLC into SCLC originates from the same alveolar type II cells (26,27).
Although the transformation of NSCLC to SCLC is a known mechanism of acquired resistance, it remains relatively rare, with the majority of cases occurring in NSCLC patients treated with EGFR-TKI. The studies involved in the above hypotheses all indicate that preexisting subpopulations of cancer cells exhibiting distinct epigenetic and transcriptomic signatures may be associated with lineage plasticity or heterogeneity under therapeutic selective pressure (28,29) (Figure 1). Single-cell sequencing of serially collected samples may help differentiate between these hypotheses. and single-cell level sequencing using serially collected samples may help to distinguish between the two hypotheses. This article synthesizes the major academic hypotheses supported by existing studies, while ruling out the possibility of a missing mixed SCLC component due to limitations in sampling methods, such as puncture or bronchoscopic biopsies, or the inefficacy of targeted and post-immunotherapy treatments.
NCSLC transformed into SCLC after EGFR-TKI treatment
T-SCLC was first reported in 2006 in a 45-year-old nonsmoking woman who showed histologic features of SCLC in a second biopsy following EGFR-TKI treatment, with a concomitant primary EGFR mutation (30). Subsequent studies of patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC who developed acquired resistance to EGFR-TKI therapy showed histologic transformation from NSCLC to SCLC in approximately 2% to 15% of cases (17,31,32). Available evidence suggests that the predominance of T-SCLC following resistance to EGFR-TKI therapy may be linked to the high prevalence of EGFR driver mutations in NSCLC.
T-SCLC shares several features with primary SCLC, including TP53/RB1 inactivation, a gene expression profile similar to that of primary SCLC, reduced or absent EGFR expression, and high sensitivity to BCL-2 family inhibitors. Extensive epigenomic reprogramming and multiple molecular alterations contribute to SCLC transformation, including the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) pathway, fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR)/Janus kinase (JAK) signaling, and activator of transcription (STAT) signaling, and key transcriptional regulatory factors such as SRY-related HMG-box 2 (SOX2) and MYC. Evidence from a few cases suggests that mutational characterization and copy number variations also change during this transition. Other data imply that the transformation of LUAD to SCLC is primarily driven by transcriptional reprogramming, rather than by genetic changes. Despite its rarity, with only a few case reports and small retrospective studies published, the frequency of NSCLC-to-SCLC transformation is expected to rise with the increasing occurrence of acquired drug resistance. However, our understanding of this transformation process and its genetic basis remains incomplete, highlighting the need for further research into the molecular mediators of therapy-induced SCLC transformation to develop appropriate interventions.
Genetic and transcriptomic changes
RB1 and TP53
The RB protein family, which includes retinoblastoma protein (pRb), p107 and p130 (encoded by the genes RB1, RBL1, and RBL2, respectively), plays a crucial role in regulating the cell cycle by binding E2F transcription factors in a complex regulatory network (33). A retrospective study (18) found that the most common features in samples transformed to SCLC were inactivation of TP53 and RB1. Offin et al. (34) observed EGFR mutations in 21% of their study participants, with 43 of them harboring both EGFR mutations and alterations in RB1 and TP53. These patients exhibited SCLC transformation after drug resistance. Niederst et al. (21) reported that RB1 loss was observed in 100% of 11 T-SCLC samples. Similarly, Xie et al. reported TP53 mutations in 100% (11/11) of samples and RB1 mutations in 33.3% (2/6) of the samples (25). Although the mutation rates of RB1/TP53 vary, they all predict a higher likelihood of histologic transformation and poorer clinical outcomes. Interestingly, TP53/RB1 mutations alone are insufficient to induce 100% transformation to SCLC (34), suggesting that additional molecular alterations or selective pressures, such as therapy, microenvironment, or hypoxia, may play a role in the transformation process.
RB1 and TP53 may be associated with large-scale genomic alterations during transformation. Genome-wide ploidy and APOBEC features were enriched in EGFR/RB1/TP53 mutant adenocarcinomas that ultimately transformed into SCLC, suggesting that these alterations occur prior to transformation and may act as early genomic determinants of lineage plasticity (34). Schaffer et al. (35) established a mouse model with triple knockout of TP53/RB1/p130 (RBL2), and they found that deletion of p130 accelerated the development induced by TP53/RB1 deletion. However, the role of p130 in T-SCLC transformation remains poorly understood. In prostate cancer, neuroendocrine transdifferentiation following treatment has been studied using a castration-resistant model (36). Deletion of TP53 was shown to induce resistance to antiandrogen therapy, while RB1 deletion mediated upregulation of epigenetic and stem-cell reprogramming factors such as enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) and SOX2. It is hypothesized that similar mechanisms may be involved in T-SCLC. Notably, when RB1/TP53 deletion was combined with phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) deletion, PTEN deletion enhanced NEtD (37,38), possibly via SOX2 upregulation. Further exploration of the mechanistic insights into RB1/TP53 loss in T-SCLC will help to elucidate the biology and ontogeny of T-SCLC, potentially leading to the identification of new therapeutic targets.
PI3K/AKT/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR)
In addition to RB1 and TP53, several studies have identified the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway as a key player in the transformation of EGFR-mutation NSCLC to SCLC (17,39). The PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway is a major promoter of cell growth, survival, and invasion in a variety of cancer types, and it has been implicated in SCLC phenotypic transformation and chemoresistance (40). Activating mutations in the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway have been found at high frequency in T-SCLC, suggesting its importance in the transformation process (41). The cancer-associated fibroblast-derived exosome microRNA-20a has been shown to promote the progression of NSCLC and chemoresistance by inhibiting the PTEN/PI3K-AKT pathway (42). Pharmacological inhibition of this pathway has been found to delay tumor growth and neuroendocrine transformation in a xenograft model of EGFR-NSCLC patients (43). Noninvasive monitoring of PI3K/AKT pathway activation, as indicated by PI3K mutations in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), could potentially alert clinicians to the onset of histological transformation before the emergence of aggressive SCLC (44).
NOTCH-ASCL1
Previous studies have demonstrated that Notch signaling plays a dual role during lung development, acting as an oncogene in neuroendocrine cells (45) while also contributing to intra-tumoral heterogeneity (46). Recent research has identified the NOTCH-ASCL1 pathway as a key process enabling T-SCLC transformation after EGFR-TKI resistance (47). Inhibition of the Notch pathway, which triggers tumor heterogeneity and treatment resistance, may offer the opportunity for personalized therapeutic strategies targeting this signaling cascade. Gene expression analysis has shown significant upregulation of Notch signaling-related genes in T-SCLC patient-derived xenografts (PDX) model, such as DLL3 and HES5 (43). ASCL1, a downstream target of Notch signaling, plays a crucial role in the transcriptional program governing neuroendocrine differentiation (48). Nouruzi et al. have demonstrated that the deletion of ASCL1 expression after estrogen receptor inhibitor treatment induces epigenetic reprogramming, affecting stem cell genes such as SOX2, Nanog homeobox (NANOG), and octamer-binding transcription factor 4 (OCT4), as well as neuroendocrine markers like CHGA and NCAM1 (49). Recent findings also suggest that ASCL1 may promote lung neuroendocrine tumor development by inhibiting extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK)1/2 signaling (50).
MYC protein
Rodarte et al. found that compared to two established genetically engineered mouse models of SCLC, prostate-like organs lacking RB1 and TP53 required MYC overexpression to form heterogeneous tumors displaying adenocarcinomatous, squamous, and neuroendocrine features (51). Gardner et al. (44) tracked the process of transformation by single-cell RNA sequencing and found that type II alveolar epithelial (ATII) cells and pulmonary neuroendocrine cells exhibit different sensitivities to MYC expression. MYC expression directly promotes the development of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells into SCLC, while ATII cells require both PTEN deletion and MYC expression for transformation. These results suggest that SCLC transformation and rapid disease progression may be driven by a combination of TP53/RB1 mutations and MYC amplification, which is commonly observed in adenocarcinomas prior to transformation (52). MYC amplification also appears in T-SCLC and NEPCs, underscoring the critical role of MYC in the early stages of transformation.
Mothers against decapentaplegic homolog 4 (SMAD4)
SMAD4, an oncogene in the transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) signaling pathway, negatively regulates epithelial cell growth. D’Haene et al. (53) reported SMAD4 mutations in T-SCLC patients, although further validation was not performed. Recently, Ding et al. (54) demonstrated that SMAD4 deletion could induce a neuroendocrine phenotype, accelerating SCLC transformation regardless of RB1 mutation status in NSCLC. Further experiments revealed that SMAD4 competes with MYC to regulate ASCL1 transcription, promoting neuroendocrine differentiation in NSCLC. Targeting MYC inhibitors may offer a potential therapeutic approach to mitigate SCLC transformation.
SOX2
SOX2, a transcription factor that plays a crucial role in determining cell fate and maintaining stem cell pluripotency and self-renewal, has been identified as a downstream molecule in the genetic and epigenetic alterations associated with NEPC development (55). Tenjin et al. reported (56) that SOX2 could be detected by immunohistochemistry and second-generation gene sequencing, and that it is regulated by SCLC ASCL1 or WNT11, which play key roles in neuroendocrine differentiation and the regulation of CDH1 expression. However, it remains unclear whether SOX is directly involved in histologic transformation to SCLC.
Other molecules
Inhibition of exportin1 has been shown to effectively suppresses SOX2 upregulation, which could potentially prevent neuroendocrine transformation in NSCLC and prostate adenocarcinoma, thus limiting aggressive tumor formation (57). Ishioka et al. (58) found that fibroblast growth factor 9 (FGF9) induced transdifferentiation of LUAD-derived cells into SCLC in a specific subpopulation of the EGFR-NSCLC cell line, upregulating its mediated FGFR pathway. This process promotes the transformation of these cells to SCLC. In another study, Quintanal-Villalon et al. (43) analyzed genomic alterations in pre- and post-transformation specimens, suggesting that genome-wide duplication events and the loss of chromosome 3p may pose potential risks for SCLC transformation. In a study by Kim et al. (59), the deletion of capping protein inhibiting regulator of actin dynamics (CRACD) was sufficient to de-repress NE-related genes in organoids and mice, with a prior study (60) showing that CRACD deletion increased tumor heterogeneity and accelerated SCLC transformation. However, the specific mechanisms behind CRACD loss of function in LUAD are still under investigation. A case report found BCL-2 overexpression in LUAD with neuroendocrine transformation compared to the initial NSCLC (61), suggesting that BCL-2 could be a key molecule in SCLC transformation. Similarly, Niederst et al. found that T-SCLC is sensitive to BCL-2 inhibitors (21).
Cell division cycle 7 (CDC7), a serine-threonine kinase, has recently been identified as an oncogenic driver of NEtD induced by targeted therapy in lung and prostate cancers. Mechanistically, CDC7 is upregulated early in NE transformation. TP53 and E2F1 may directly regulate CDC7 transcription by binding to its gene promoter (62). Therefore, CDC7 represents a promising therapeutic target to control lineage plasticity and NEtD. Its upregulation contributes to acquired resistance to targeted therapies in lung and prostate cancers.
In conclusion, genetic alterations during transformation do not occur in isolation. The loss of TP53 and RB1 is a prerequisite for NE transformation. These alterations often coexist with a multitude of biological events, with the molecules interacting and cooperating to drive histological transformation. Understanding these complex mechanisms is crucial for developing therapeutic strategies that address the underlying biology of transformation.
Epigenetic characterization
In addition to genomic alterations, several epigenetic abnormalities, primarily histone modifications such as methylation, acetylation, and ubiquitination, play a direct role in genealogical plasticity and neuroendocrine reprogramming. These epigenetic alterations involve complex interactions between DNA methylation and histone modifications, which together regulate chromatin accessibility and drive aberrant transcription.
Histone methylation
EZH2, an enzyme subunit of polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), catalyzes the trimethylation of histone H3 at Lys27 (H3K27me3), and is frequently overexpressed in several cancer types. In NEPC, it was discovered that MYCN binds to EZH2, enhancing H3K27me3 methylation, thereby following prostate cancer to escape androgen receptor dependence and facilitating the evolution of NEPC (63). While EZH2 expression does not significantly differ in large-cell lung carcinomas, LUAD, and squamous-cell lung carcinomas, it is markedly elevated in SCLC (64). In SCLC, EZH2 has been shown to inhibit lineage-specific transformation by suppressing lineage-specific factors (44,65). Notably, AXL and YAP1 are expressed in non-NE-SCLC isoforms, indicating that EZH2 plays a key role in lineage plasticity in both prostate cancer and SCLC-NEtD (66). Euchromatin histone lysine methyltransferase 2 (EHMT2), also known as G9a, is a histone 3 lysine 9 (H3K9) methyltransferase that mediates monomethylation and demethylation of H3K9 residues. Overexpression of G9a has been observed in various cancers, and inhibitors targeting G9a are being developed as potential therapeutic drugs (67). Recently, Yang et al. (68) identified G9a as an epigenetic driver of LUAD-to-SCLC transformation. Mechanistically, EHMT2 increases methylation of the SFRP1 promoter region, reducing SFRP1 expression, which activates the WNT/β-catenin pathway and triggers TKI-mediated NE transformation. The combination of the G9a inhibitor UNC0642 with erlotinib was found to significantly reverse SCLC transformation and exert synergistic anti-tumor effects in vivo. Zhang et al. have shown (69) that G9a and EZH2 interact and promote the silencing of SMAD4, thereby activating the ERK/c-MYC signaling pathway. Among them, SU08, a compound targeting EZH2 and G9a, sensitized drug-resistant cells to therapeutic agents by modulating the SMAD4/ERK/c-MYC axis. These findings shed light on the mechanisms underlying drug resistance and strategies to reverse drug resistance in NSCLC. In conclusion, histone methyltransferases play a significant role in driving the development of NEtD, enhancing the understanding of histologic transformation in lung cancer and the mechanisms of resistance to EGFR-TKI.
Histone demethylation (HDM)
Lysine-specific demethylase 1 (KDM1A), also known as LSD1, is a HDM that specifically targets H3K4me1/2, which is highly upregulated in SCLC (70). In SCLC, a messenger RNA (mRNA)-binding protein (ZFP36L1), whose expression is restored upon binding to an LSD1 inhibitor, binds to SOX2 and INSM1, blocking the neuroendocrine differentiation and inducing a non-neuroendocrine “inflammatory” phenotype. This highlights how the stability of regulatory lineage mRNAs can control the transition from neuroendocrine to non-neuroendocrine transcription, demonstrating the role of mRNA stability in regulating neuroendocrine plasticity (71). In SCLC, LSD1 inhibition downregulates ASCL1 and neuroendocrine differentiation. The downregulation of ASCL1 correlates with increased sensitivity to LSD1 inhibitors in cell lines and PDX models (70). Similarly, inhibition of lysine demethylase 5A (KDM5A) or the histone demethylase family also inhibits ASCL1 expression (72). KDM5A, also known as RBP2 or JARID1A, functions as a demethylase targeting H3K4me1. A mouse model of SCLC was established by Oser et al. (72), suggesting that KDM5A maintains ASCL1 levels and neuroendocrine differentiation by inhibiting NOTCH2 and NOTCH target genes. Furthermore, combining KDM5A inhibitors with LSD1 inhibitors has been shown to synergistically inhibit ASCL1 expression in SCLC cancer cell lines. However, beyond the inhibition of ASCL1 and NOTCH, the exact mechanisms behind why only certain SCLC cases are sensitive to LSD1 inhibition and how LSD1 and KDM5A promote SCLC neuroendocrine transdifferentiation and survival remain unclear.
Histone acetylation
Histone deacetylases (HDACs) play a crucial role in the epigenetic regulation of gene expression by remodeling chromatin. Isoenzymes of the HDAC family exhibit dysregulated expression across a wide variety of cancers (73). A recent study by Li et al. (74) suggests that histological transformation of NSCLC may result from epigenetic alterations within tumor cells, with HDAC10/HDAC1 being a key regulator that is downregulated during transformation. Previous studies reported (75,76) that the combination of HDAC and EZH2 inhibitors killed castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), leading to significant tumor regression by upregulating the stress-responsive transcription factor ATF3 in a CRPC mouse model. Recently, Oh et al. (11) demonstrated that the HDAC inhibitor fimepinostat restores EGFR expression in SNU-2962A cells and its organoid model, enhancing the sensitivity of SCLC to EGFR-TKI in ex vivo models. Overall, these findings suggest that HDACs play a significant role in the progression of NEtD and identify HDAC inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy for patients with EGFR-mutant LUADs and NEtD.
In summary, epigenetic modifications, particularly histone methylation, demethylation, and acetylation, are key players in the regulation of neuroendocrine transformation in cancers such as LUAD and SCLC. Targeting these pathways may provide valuable therapeutic opportunities for overcoming resistance and controlling histological plasticity.
NCSLC transformed into SCLC following targeted therapy
It is important to note that most histological transformations currently observed occur in patients with EGFR mutations. However, case reports have shown that SCLC transformation can also occur after treatment with ALK-TKIs (77,78) and ROS1-TKIs (79), implying that SCLC transformation is not exclusive to EGFR-mutated NSCLC.
Sequist and colleagues found no instances of transformation to SCLC among 79 surgical specimens from stage III NSCLC patients treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy (17), suggesting that EGFR wild-type NSCLC has a lower probability of undergoing SCLC transformation compared to EGFR mutant NSCLC. A comprehensive analysis of a large SCLC cohort (39) detected other recurrent NSCLC-associated oncogenic driver mutations including ALK (n=5), RET (n=5), ROS1 (n=3), and NTRK1 (n=1) fusions, albeit in small numbers. This suggests that transformation to SCLC is not unique to EGFR-mutated NSCLC, and coexisting mutations and epigenetic alterations in these cases may share similarities with the EGFR mutant T-SCLC cohort. It has been shown that NSCLC patients with ALK fusion mutations develop an ALK fusion V1180L mutation and convert to SCLC after acquired resistance to alectinib (80). Therefore, in patients with poor responses to ALK-TKIs, the possibility of both resistance mutations and SCLC transformation should be considered. Multi-omics analysis of lung cancer has shown a reduced frequency of KRAS mutations in pre-conversion LUADs, which may indicate that KRAS-mutant LUADs are unlikely to undergo neuroendocrine transformation. This could also be due to the historical lack of effective KRAS-targeted inhibitors (43).
NSCLC to SCLC transformation after immunotherapy
Histological transformation has been widely reported in advanced NSCLC after EGFR-TKI resistance, but it can also occur after immunotherapy resistance, although this phenomenon is less common and often under-recognized, leading to under-diagnosis and misdiagnosis. The frequency of transformation remains unclear; the first case was reported in 2017, and by 2021, fewer than 20 cases had been documented. Studies on NSCLC to SCLC transformation after immunotherapy resistance, such as those by Iams et al. (81), Bar et al. (4), and Hsu et al. (82) have identified mutations in TP53, RB1, and FBXW7 (Arg441Phe), but the specific molecular mechanism remains unclear. The main challenge may be the low frequency of re-biopsy after immunotherapy (83). Therefore, in the era of tumor immunotherapy, the importance of rebiopsy and molecular targeted therapy should be emphasized.
Treatment
Although research on the molecular mechanisms of T-SCLC is rapidly advancing, the clinical translational significance of these findings is still unclear. In the context of acquired resistance to targeted therapies in lung cancer, there are no large-scale clinical studies providing effective treatment strategies for patients presenting with histologic transformation. Multiple lines of evidence suggest (84,85) that plasma gastrin-releasing peptide precursor (ProGRP), neuron-specific enolase (NSE), and cytokeratin 19 fragment (CYFRA21-1) assays can identify SCLC transformation and NSCLC patients at high risk of transformation. In addition, TP53 and RB1 deletions have been identified as risk signs for NSCLC to SCLC transformation.
The increase in rebiopsies of tumors after recurrence, along with improved isolation and identification of NEPC tumor cells from peripheral blood, has enhanced our ability to identify such cases and provided a foundation for the design of some clinical studies. Standardized treatment
Clinical outcomes after transformation are similar to those of primary SCLC, with rapid progression on TKI therapy and transient responses to SCLC chemotherapy. The most comprehensive analysis of treatment responses in converted cases to date comes from the retrospective multicenter study by Marcoux et al. (5), which showed that T-SCLC occurred within 17.8 months of primary tumor diagnosis. The most commonly used regimens were platinum-etoposide (54%) and paclitaxel regimens (50%). After transformation, the median progression-free survival (mPFS) and OS were 3.4 and 2.7 months, respectively, with a median OS of 10.9 months, which were comparable to the results for conventional extensive-stage SCLC (mPFS, 5.5 months; OS, 9.6 months). In contrast, the 17 patients who received immunotherapy (including anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4 agents, or their combinations) had no clinical response, suggesting a lower response rate to immune checkpoint inhibitors in T-SCLC or EGFR-mutated adenocarcinomas. Reports by Nishikawa et al. (86) and Tokaca et al. (87) also showed that nivolumab did not achieve clinical benefit. However, a recent study of 47 patients with EGFR-mutated T-SCLC found that PD-L1 inhibitors in combination with chemotherapy ± bevacizumab may be a potentially safe option for patients with T-SCLC harboring the EGFR L858R mutation (88). After disease progression, the benefit of continuing EGFR-TKI combination chemotherapy remains unclear due to transformation to SCLC. In a retrospective study (8), SCLC transformed after EGFR-TKI failure, treated with EP plus amlotinib, achieved mPFS of 9.0 months and mOS of 14.0 months, which were broadly convergent with the results reported in the ACTION-2 prospective study. These findings suggest that the combination of etoposide + carboplatin with amlotinib may be a potential therapeutic strategy. These findings suggest that chemotherapy in combination with a TKI is also an effective treatment option.
The treatment of T-SCLC remains complex, and as of now, there is no effective treatment specifically for T-SCLC. Most clinical studies are based on the treatment of typical SCLC, and effective treatments for T-SCLC are still being explored. The therapeutic effects of most drugs are temporary, with only a small percentage of patients responding to specific therapies, requiring continuous adjustment of treatment regimens to explore the optimal combinations of therapeutic agents.
Potential treatment options
Due to rapid relapse after chemotherapy, new treatment options are being explored. However, data on alternative therapies for translational disease remain limited, and no randomized or prospective trials have been completed.
For patients with advanced triple mutant EGFR/TP53/RB1, an ongoing clinical trial (NCT03567642) is exploring an interventional strategy to investigate the feasibility of first-line chemotherapy with osimertinib in combination with etoposide-platinum chemotherapy to eliminate or maximize inhibition of the putative precursor clone in T-SCLC. This approach has yielded a response rate of 54% with a PFS of 4 months (5). In this context, BCL-2 family protein inhibitors can be used to block progression. ABT-263 (navitoclax), an orally bioavailable inhibitor of BCL-2 and BCL-XL, has shown greater sensitivity in NSCLC after resistance to EGFR-TKIs (21), inducing a strong apoptotic response. Despite the lack of clinical trials, this combination shows great potential.
Targeting the cell cycle vulnerability arising from RB1 loss could also counteract SCLC transformation, which is more sensitive to a variety of drugs. For example, LY3295668, a highly specific AURKA inhibitor, has been shown to kill RB1-deficient cancer cells while sparing normal cells (89,90). Additionally, EZH2 inhibitors have been found to inhibit neuroendocrine transformation in preclinical models of SCLC (36). These findings suggest that targeting cancer cells containing genetic alterations driving plasticity could potentially eliminate emerging cancer-spectrum plasticity. A study also (62) support the use of CDC7 inhibitors like simurosertib (NCT03261947) to induce MYC proteasome degradation, inhibiting NE transformation and prolonging adenocarcinoma response to treatment. Moreover, inhibiting MYC in the presence of SMAD4 deficiency has been shown to increase sensitivity to MYC inhibitors, making them a promising targeted therapy for NSCLC (54). Redin et al. also suggest that SMARCA4 could regulate state plasticity in SCLC by controlling ASCL1 and REST splicing (91). Inhibition of SMARCA4 expression could drive ERBB pathway activation in SCLC, sensitizing tumors to afatinib and providing a novel therapeutic approach for T-SCLC.
A number of therapies that have achieved significant clinical efficacy in non-T-SCLC have now also been evaluated for T-SCLC. Lurbinectedin, approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a second-line treatment for recurrent metastatic or advanced SCLC (92), has demonstrated strong anti-tumor effects in T-SCLC (93), especially when combined with Osimertinib, which is commonly used for patients with T790M mutation-resistant NSCLC (94). Almonertinib, a third-line agent for recurrent SCLC, has also shown favorable efficacy in T-SCLC patients (18). Furthermore, inhibition of chromosomal region maintenance 1 (XPO1) can sensitize SCLC to chemotherapy (57), and recent study (95) suggested that selinexor (an exportin1 inhibitor) downregulates SOX2 and NE dedifferentiation in T-SCLC, which may offer a potential therapeutic strategy to limit spectral plasticity and prevent or treat NE transformation in both lung and prostate cancers.
Previous studies have shown that EGFR expression is reduced in T-SCLC with or without treatment with TKIs compared to EGFR-NSCLC that is about to transform, and clinical studies have demonstrated that BET inhibitors (AZD5153, birabresib, molibresib, and JQ1) could inhibit cell growth by downregulating MYC expression, while HDAC inhibitors like fimepinostat and other epigenetic modifiers can restore EGFR expression in T-SCLC models, potentially resensitizing these tumors to EGFR-TKIs (11). Based on the foundation of the previous study, we are looking forward to more related clinical studies to explore the optimal clinical treatment strategies.
Conclusions
The histological transformation of NSCLC to SCLC reveals remarkable tumor plasticity and complexity of drug resistance mechanisms. Current studies have clarified that inactivation of TP53/RB1 is a central driver of this transformation, and its mutation or deletion serves as a key molecular marker to predict the risk of transformation. Neuroendocrine differentiation features such as ASCL1, SYP, CHGA expression, and epigenetic abnormalities such as CDKN2A hypermethylation and EZH2 overexpression further elucidated the molecular basis of tumor lineage plasticity. Liquid biopsy techniques, such as dynamic monitoring of ctDNA, have shown potential in tracking the evolution of drug-resistant clones and identifying early warning signals of transformation, particularly in SCLC-associated mutations like MYC amplification in ctDNA following drug resistance. The enrichment of mutations such as MYC amplification and NOTCH pathway inactivation may precede imaging progression, providing a window period for early intervention.
Although chemotherapy remains the first-line treatment option for T-SCLC, its efficacy is limited, and patient prognosis is inferior. Although combination treatment strategies such as chemotherapy combined with EGFR-TKIs can prolong progression-free survival, most of the existing studies are small-sample retrospective analyses and lack in-depth support for translational mechanisms. In clinical practice, the insufficient application of secondary biopsy and molecular typing often leads to a diagnostic lag, and the adjuvant role of plasma markers such as ProGRP and NSE has not yet been fully realized. It is recommended to routinely detect TP53, RB1, KRAS, ASCL1, MYC, and parallel immunohistochemical detection of CD56 and synaptophysin during the baseline screening period in patients with advanced NSCLC, especially those with EGFR/ALK mutations and a history of smoking. For clinical practice, it is recommended to shorten the interval between computed tomography (CT) evaluations to 1–2 months and to combine with the metabolic profile of positron emission tomography (PET)-CT to improve the early lesion detection rate, and dynamically monitor the evolution of drug-resistant clones through longitudinal liquid biopsies such as cell-free DNA (cfDNA)/ctDNA to achieve risk stratification and early warning.
The poor prognosis of T-SCLC emphasizes the importance of preventing transformation, detecting transformation, and providing individualized treatment after transformation. First, identify potential risk groups through molecular profiling to clarify the transformation driving mechanism; second, capture the clonal evolution trajectory through intensive dynamic monitoring to track the molecular signature variation in real time; and lastly, implement early intervention at the critical nodes of transformation to block the malignant process. However, there is a lot of room for development in all aspects of the process, and future research should focus on analyzing the causal relationship between TP53/RB1 inactivation and neuroendocrine phenotypic transformation, conducting prospective studies to verify the clinical prediction efficacy of molecular markers, and integrating multi-dimensional data from the genome, epigenome, imaging and liquid biopsy, with the aim of further elucidating the mechanism of T-SCLC transformation, and then formulating a detailed individualized We hope to further elucidate the mechanism of T-SCLC transformation, so as to formulate detailed individualized treatment plans and improve the prognosis of patients.
